cases.final_diagnosis: CNC-02 has an isolated mechanical vibration fault, most consistent with a bearing/spindle wear issue: its vibration stepped up from a mean of 4.074 mm/s (ticks 840-899) to 4.311 mm/s (ticks 900-920), peaked at 4.577 mm/s above the 4.50 mm/s setpoint, and produced two vibration alarms (tick 914 at 4.58 mm/s and tick 919 at 4.51 mm/s). CNC-02 load, power, and temperature are normal, and peer machines CNC-05, CNC-06, CNC-07, and CNC-08 all run far lower (about 1.5-2.7 mm/s), so this is not a line-wide problem; CNC-04 did show a step-up around tick 909 but remains well below alarm level and does not explain the CNC-02 alarms. This supports H1 over H2 and H3.

CNC-05 has a genuine developing mechanical fault, not a sensor noise or job-normal condition. Vibration is above the 4.50 mm/s alarm setpoint and still climbing after the 10-tick wait: tick 840 = 4.425 mm/s, mean 4.527 over ticks 840-844, mean 4.674 over ticks 845-849, and 4.979 mm/s at tick 850 (E21). This is unique to CNC-05: CNC-01, CNC-02, CNC-03 and CNC-04 all run at roughly 1.5-2.5 mm/s over the same windows (E4, E5, E8, E16, E19). CNC-05's own power (~12.4-12.9 kW, E12), load (~66-71%, E15) and temperature (~147-148, E6) stayed flat, ruling out an operating-change cause (H1), and the continued elevation after the wait and across jobs contradicts H3 (job-normal vibration). H2 is therefore supported. The exact faulty subsystem (bearing/spindle, feed-axis servo drive, or hydraulics - hydraulic pressure dipped to 66.8 bar at tick 840 vs ~68-70 bar earlier, E18) is not isolated, so no single named repair meets the 0.90 intervention threshold.

Pending one discriminating measurement: comparing CNC-06 vibration during the passed job-14 machining window (1228-1293) versus the failed job-15 window (1296-1363). If vibration is comparably high during job 14, H3 (CNC-06 vibration damage) is contradicted and H1 (bad batch-2 material lot) becomes favored; if job 14 ran at low vibration while job 15 ran high, H3 is supported.

Out-of-spec incoming material on batch 2 is causing the inspection failures: jobs 11-13 (batch 2) all failed inspection (0 of 3 passed) while every batch 1 job 1-10 passed (10 of 10) (E7, E3). The route machines CNC-01 through CNC-06 show no abnormal vibration, load, or following_error trace and no equipment alarm during the batch-2 window (E8-E15; CNC-06 is idle), and job 10 passed the same stations (CNC-03/04/05/06) just before job 11 failed on them, which argues against a persistent equipment fault (H2). This is H1 (batch-2 material lot out of spec), not an equipment fault.

The inspection failures are not explained by a CNC-04 or CNC-01 vibration fault. CNC-04 vibration stepped up after tick 181 and stayed high (bucket means roughly 1.6-2.4) through all four jobs, yet job 3 passed inspection after running CNC-04 during ticks 324-386 in that same high-vibration band (E13, E14, E7). CNC-01 was also running at high vibration while job 3 was machined on it (E10 maxima about 2.09-2.20 in buckets 121-180, covering job 3's CNC-01 window 127-185), and job 3 still passed (E10, E14, E7). So a spindle/bearing fault on CNC-01 or CNC-04 would also have rejected job 3; those stations are exonerated. CNC-02, CNC-03 and CNC-05 show no comparable window that is bad for jobs 1, 2 and 4 but good for job 3 (E6, E11, E12, E3). The failures instead cluster by inspection time - fail at ticks 324, 396 and 547, pass at 471 (E7, E19) - which is consistent with inspection instrument/tolerance drift (H2). Per the manual (E15/E2), none of the four approved repairs (bearing replacement, speed reset, servo-drive replacement, hydraulic seal repair) fixes an inspection instrument, material or tooling, so no CNC intervention is indicated. Leading hypothesis: H2 (inspection-related), not instrument-confirmed; H1 and H3 are effectively exonerated by job 3.

Intermittent inspection failures are confined to batch 2 (jobs 14, 19, 20 failed; jobs 11-13 and 15-18 passed; all of batch 1 passed). No single CNC machine is implicated: vibration is broadly elevated and comparable across all seven machines rather than unique to one station, and the failing job 14 traversed all seven machines while passing batch-2 jobs used subsets (e.g., job 15 used CNC-04 to CNC-07, job 16 used CNC-03 and CNC-04), so CNC-03 through CNC-07 appear in both passing and failing routes. This pattern fits nonuniform batch-2 material/process conditions with healthy machines, not a repairable machine fault (H2).

CNC-02's following_error spiked to 20.10 µm at tick 1358, just above the 20.00 µm alarm threshold, then immediately returned to normal (19.35 µm at tick 1359, 18.85 µm at tick 1360) and stayed near 18.85 µm afterward. This was a single-tick transient excursion, not a persistent fault. All other running machines (CNC-01, CNC-03, CNC-04, CNC-06, CNC-07) show following_error far below the threshold, with the highest maximum about 6.54 µm on CNC-06; CNC-05 is idle with no fault signal; and no other alarms occurred. Because there is no active fault, no repair (bearing, servo drive, hydraulics, or setting reset) is warranted, and intervening on a cleared transient would not fix anything.

CNC-05 has a progressive physical hydraulic pressure leak, most consistent with leaking hydraulic seals (a weakening pump or sticking relief valve remains possible per manual §2.15). Its hydraulic pressure fell continuously from a mean of 63.102 bar (ticks 1000–1014) to 56.598 bar (ticks 1285–1290) while the machine sat idle, and readings at ticks 1290–1300 remain low at roughly 56–58 bar with repeated alarms below the 55 bar setpoint (54.29 bar at tick 1281, 54.99 bar at tick 1288). The pressure does not self-recover. CNC-02, the only other hydraulics-equipped machine, stays flat near 68–69 bar, so this is isolated to CNC-05, not a factory-wide supply problem. Samples are continuous with no gaps (E4, E8), which argues against a transducer fault (H2), and the repeated low readings rule out a one-off transient (H3).
